power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Number personification (NP), the attribution of gender, age, or character to digits, is common among 9-to 12-year-olds, but its relationship to other forms of childhood personification remains unknown.
Because NP and imaginary companions (ICs) share the attribution of personhood to non-living entities and high idiosyncrasy, we hypothesized that NP is a developmental extension of ICs.
In a web survey, 2,193 Japanese mothers of children in grades 1-6 reported their child's current and past IC and NP status and fantasy orientation.
Current ICs were reported for 15.1% of children, and current NP for 1.2%.
Contrary to our hypothesis, past IC did not predict current NP; instead, children with a current IC had four times the odds of NP (odds ratio = 4.16).
Grade, gender, and fantasy orientation were related to ICs but not, or only weakly, to NP.
NP appears to co-occur with ICs rather than to follow them developmentally.
It is generally known that children tend to attribute personification to various objects (Piaget, 1929).
text.formatted: It is generally known that children tend to attribute personification to various objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Piaget, 1929)</ref>.

text.text: Young children personify everything in their expressions (e.g., "The wall feels it's being knocked on.
") As they grow older, personification is observed in objects that move autonomously (e.g., "The moon knows it's moving.").

Even when they understand that an object is inanimate, they still attribute personality traits to it and interact with it with care and affection, as if it is truly alive (Piaget, 1929; Singer and Singer, 1990; Taylor and Mottweiler, 2008; Moriguchi and Shinohara, 2012; Lin et al., 2016; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: "An imaginary companion" (IC) is defined as an invisible character with a specific name that exists for a period of at least several months.
This character is referenced in the child's daily conversations, plays with the child, and is perceived by the child as a real presence (Svendsen, 1934).

text.text: Recent studies have expanded the concept of IC to include not only invisible friends (IF) but also personified objects (PO), such as dolls or stuffed animals treated as real friends (Singer and Singer, 1990).

text.text: A case study describes a child with an IC named "Ume-chan," an invisible girl who taught her various things (Moriguchi and Shinohara, 2012).

text.text: The prevalence of ICs varies across cultures but is particularly high in preschool years.

In Western countries, about 50% of preschool children are reported to have IFs (Pearson et al., 2001; Boerger et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2016), whereas in Japan, approximately 40% have POs and 8% have IFs (Moriguchi and Shinohara, 2012; Motoshima et al., 2014; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: ICs are most frequently observed between ages 2 and 6, peaking around age 4, and then gradually decline as children enter school age (Pearson et al., 2001; Boerger et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2016; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017). Matsuda et al. (2018) found that even abstract concepts such as numbers can be personified-a phenomenon known as Number Personification (NP).

(2018)</ref> found that even abstract concepts such as numbers can be personified-a phenomenon known as Number Personification (NP).

text.text: They asked 151 children aged 9 to 12 and 55 adults to assign personality traits (gender, age, morality, and sociability, each with a "none" option) to each of the ten digits, twice with a one-month interval, and used the temporal consistency of the responses as an indicator of NP.

The younger group (ages 9-10) showed high temporal consistency, which diminished with age in the older group (ages 11-12) and in adults; with age, participants increasingly chose "none" instead of specific traits, indicating the disappearance of NP.
NP is of interest beyond its curiosity value.

In the learning of abstract concepts, linking them to familiar and concrete knowledge is argued to help children grasp what abstract symbols stand for (Fyfe and Nathan, 2019); NP may represent one such link, in which abstract numbers are connected to children's familiar knowledge about people, and it has been suggested to aid the discrimination of numbers and the understanding of relations among them (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: However, little is known about which children show NP and how it arises.
To address this question, we focus on the most extensively studied form of personification in childhood, the imaginary companion.
Taken together, these lines of research indicate that NP and IC share two features.
The first is that both involve attributing personhood to entities that are not alive.
The second is idiosyncrasy.

As the cases of "Ume-chan" and "Totoro" illustrate, each child creates an IC of his or her own, and the same holds for NP: for the digit "2," one child may report a masculine impression while another reports a feminine one (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: There is also some evidence that children with ICs more readily attribute mental states to animals and inanimate objects (Tahiroglu and Taylor, 2019).

text.text: These similarities motivate the hypothesis that IC and NP are two expressions of the same imaginative disposition, placed at different points of development.

Both can be regarded as forms of children's fantasy play, that is, play in which children act on an imagined rather than a real state of affairs, of which fantasy orientation is a general measure (Singer and Singer, 1990; Taylor and Carlson, 1997).

text.text: The preschool years are regarded as the "high season" of fantasy orientation, during which ICs are most frequently observed (Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: NP, which emerges after school entry and is directed at an abstract rather than a concrete target, may therefore reflect a more developed form of fantasy orientation in the school-age years (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: On this view, NP would not be an isolated curiosity but the school-age continuation of the same imaginative disposition that gives rise to ICs in preschoolers.
The present study tested the hypothesis that NP is a developmental extension of IC, predicting that children who currently show NP would be more likely to have a history of ICs.

In addition, the presence of IC is known to vary with age, gender, and fantasy orientation, the latter being an individual's tendency to think and play in imaginative contexts (Singer and Singer, 1990; Taylor et al., 1993; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: We therefore built a model predicting current NP status from these factors in order to clarify how NP arises.
A web-based survey was administered to 2,193 parents of elementary school children.

Because directly questioning children imposes considerable practical constraints, children's ICs have traditionally been studied through parental report (Bouldin and Pratt, 1999; Manosevitz et al., 1973; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

Each participant was asked to provide information about one of her children.

Although the study was advertised as a survey on "elementary school children's personification in their surroundings," many respondents reported on children who were not in elementary school (preschool: 1,629 cases; junior high school or older: 1,850 cases).
These cases were excluded from the analysis.
Additionally, 328 responses were excluded due to incomplete or invalid data.
The most common reason for exclusion was selecting "don't know" or "none" in the questions regarding fantasy orientation (described later).
After these exclusions, responses from 2,193 participants were analyzed (mean age of mothers = 39.6 years, SD = 4.8; all female).
We examined the demographic profiles of the excluded 328 cases and did not find systematic differences in child age or gender compared with the included group (Table 1).

An internet-based questionnaire was conducted.
All procedures were carried out in Japanese.
The questionnaire was composed of four parts that corresponded to four themes: 1) background information (child's age, gender, and birth order), 2) IC, 3) NP, and 4) fantasy orientation.
In the questionnaire, participants are required to answer all questions.
The following are the details.
First part: Background information on the age and gender of their children was asked.
Second part: We asked parents to describe their children's ICs.
We explained to parents about IC by providing the following example based on the previous work on IC (Moriguchi and Todo, 2017): Sat-chan, who is a 6-year-old girl, has a dear friend named 'ai-chan.'
text.formatted: We explained to parents about IC by providing the following example based on the previous work on IC <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Moriguchi and Todo, 2017)</ref>: Sat-chan, who is a 6-year-old girl, has a dear friend named 'ai-chan.'

text.text: Ai-chan is not a real child but a teddy bear.
One day, she told the teddy bear, 'I will go out with my mother.
So, please be a good girl, Ai-chan.
Here are cookies for a tea break.
Feel free to take some.'
Then, she made the bear sit on the chair, put some cookies on the table, and went out with her mother."
We asked parents whether their children currently or previously played like the example above, with puppets and dolls as if they were human friends.

If the parents answered the question affirmatively, we asked them to provide further information: (a) the age of the children when the IC appeared and disappeared, and (b) a specific description of ICs (puppets, dolls, or imaginary beings), including age, gender, and name.
Third part: We asked parents to describe the children's NP.
We explained to parents about NP by providing the following examples based on the previous research (Matsuda et al., 2018): "Number 1 is an energetic girl, and numbers 2 and 3 are siblings.
text.formatted: We explained to parents about NP by providing the following examples based on the previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Matsuda et al., 2018)</ref>: "Number 1 is an energetic girl, and numbers 2 and 3 are siblings.

text.text: Number 4 is a female who always cares about other numbers."
We asked parents whether their children currently or previously attributed such personality traits to numbers.

If parents answered affirmatively, we asked them to provide further information (a) the age of the children when the NP appeared and disappeared, and (b) a specific description of NPs (gender, personality, age, goodness, body shape, relationship, social status).
Fourth part: We asked parents about fantasy orientation.

The questionnaire consisted of 5 open-ended questions on the child's favorite solitary game, favorite game with other children, favorite story, favorite toy, and favorite TV show, and two forced-choice questions on children's tendency to pretend to be animals or other people, and children's private speech before going to sleep (Singer, 1973; Taylor and Carlson, 1997; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: ICs were classified into PO and IF based on the responses describing the type of IC.
If a physical object, such as a "stuffed animal" or "doll" was mentioned, it was classified as PO.
If the response included terms like "imaginary" or "invisible," it was classified as IF.
In addition, responses that did not mention a physical object but instead described a character, such as "Maria, a girl" or "a fairy" were also classified as IF.
Vague responses like "various" were not classified into either category.
If both PO and IF were mentioned, such as "a stuffed animal and an imaginary character," the response was counted in both categories.
Therefore, the sum of IF and PO does not necessarily equal the total IC count as depicted in Table 2.

For the analysis of fantasy orientation, the answers to the five open-ended questions were classified as either fantasy-oriented or reality-oriented, based on the schema given by Taylor and Carlson (1997).

text.text: For example, the answers to the favorite game with other children were coded as fantasy-oriented (e.g., pretend play) or reality-oriented (e.g., chase game).

Video games and game consoles (e.g., "Nintendo Switch") were coded as realityoriented, because the questionnaire did not allow us to determine whether the child engaged in imaginative play through them.
Answers that could not be classified (e.g., "nothing in particular") did not add to the score.
All answers were coded independently by two coders: the first author and a master's student who was blind to the hypotheses and to the children's IC and NP status.
Of the 10,965 answers (2,193 children × 5 questions), 10,667 (97.3%) were coded by both coders; inter-rater agreement on these answers was high (agreement = 94.4%, Cohen's κ = .88).
The first author's codes were used in the main analyses, and the analyses were repeated with the second coder's codes as a sensitivity check (Section 3.4).

We calculated the score of fantasy orientation as the summation of (1) the number of answers classified as fantasy-oriented among the five open-ended questions and (2) the number of affirmative answers among the two forced-choice questions (ranging from 0-7).
Among 2,193 parental answers, 331 (15.1%) answered that their children currently have ICs, and 274 (12.5%) had ICs in the past.
On the other hand, 26 (1.2%) responded that their children currently have NPs, while 10 (0.5%) had NPs in the past.

School grade, gender, fantasy orientation scores, current IC status, and past IC status were entered as predictors.
Past NP status was not included because current and past NP were mutually exclusive response options in the questionnaire.
The results are summarized in Table 4.

text.text: The presence of a current IC was the strongest predictor of NP (β = 1.42, SE = 0.468, z = 3.04, p = .002).

This corresponds to an odds ratio of e1.42 ≈ 4.16 (95% CI [1.66, 10.40]), indicating that children who currently have ICs were about four times more likely to also show NP compared to those without ICs.

Fantasy orientation was also a significant positive predictor (β = 0.320, SE = 0.134, z = 2.38, p = .017, OR = 1.38 per point, 95% CI [1.06, 1.79]), whereas school grade (p = .825), gender (p = .824), and past IC status (p = .567) were not significant predictors.
Adding two-way interactions did not improve the model fit (AIC increased from 269.7 to 278.8).

In summary, logistic regression confirmed that NP was most strongly associated with the presence of current ICs, with an additional, smaller contribution of fantasy orientation; demographic variables did not predict NP.
This result highlights the importance of IC experience as a proximal factor for the emergence of NP, consistent with the correlational analyses.
We repeated the partial correlation and logistic regression analyses using the second coder's classification of fantasy orientation.

The pattern of results was unchanged: in the partial correlations, current NP was associated with current IC (r = .092, p < .001) but not with fantasy orientation (r = .029, p = .168); in the logistic regression, current IC (β = 1.47, p = .002, OR = 4.35) and fantasy orientation (β = 0.287, p = .034, OR = 1.33) remained significant predictors of current NP, and no other predictor was significant.

text.text: We also re-estimated the logistic regression with household income (band midpoint, in millions of yen) added as a covariate, because socioeconomic status was not part of our hypotheses but was available.
The effects of current IC (β = 1.38, p = .004, OR = 3.99) and fantasy orientation (β = 0.312, p = .022, OR = 1.37) were essentially unchanged.

Household income itself showed a small positive association with current NP (β = 0.091 per million yen, SE = 0.040, p = .025, OR = 1.10), whereas it was unrelated to current IC (p = .35) and fantasy orientation (Spearman's ρ = .008).

Given the small number of children with NP and the fact that the prevalence of NP did not increase monotonically across income terciles (1.1%, 0.9%, and 1.8%), we do not interpret this association further.
This study aimed to test the hypothesis that number personification (NP) in schoolage children may represent a developmental extension of imaginary companions (IC).
Specifically, we predicted that children who had experienced ICs in the past would be more likely to show NP in the present.
To examine this, we conducted a large-scale web survey of 2,193 parents, assessing their children's current and past IC status, current NP status, and fantasy orientation.
Contrary to our hypothesis, the analyses did not reveal a significant association between past IC and current NP.
Instead, NP was associated with the presence of current ICs.
The adjusted odds of current NP were 4.16 times as high for children with a current IC as for those without one, whereas past IC did not predict current NP.
The latter finding warrants caution: current NP was reported for only 26 children, and mothers had to recall ICs that may have ended several years earlier.
Nevertheless, the pattern across the partial correlations is informative.
Past NP (n = 10) was associated with past IC and, more weakly, with current IC, whereas current NP was associated only with current IC (Table 3).
text.formatted: Past NP (n = 10) was associated with past IC and, more weakly, with current IC, whereas current NP was associated only with current IC (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: That is, NP was linked to IC of the same period rather than to IC of an earlier period.

This pattern is more consistent with NP and IC co-occurring than with NP succeeding IC, although our cross-sectional design cannot establish whether IC typically precedes NP or whether the two experiences begin and end together within an individual child.

The age-related decline in NP reported by Matsuda et al. (2018) and the lower prevalence of current IC in the higher grades of our sample likewise describe differences between age groups rather than within-child change.

text.text: In addition, NP showed no significant partial correlations with school grade, gender, or fantasy orientation, although fantasy orientation had a small positive effect on NP when the other variables were controlled in the logistic regression.
IC, on the other hand, was clearly related to these factors: it was more frequent in younger children, in girls than in boys, and in children with higher fantasy orientation.
Likewise, fantasy orientation itself decreased with school grade and was higher in girls.

Both of these patterns, for IC and for fantasy orientation, align with previous research (e.g., Moriguchi and Todo, 2017) and indicate that the present dataset is consistent with established findings on IC and fantasy play.
text.formatted: Both of these patterns, for IC and for fantasy orientation, align with previous research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Moriguchi and Todo, 2017)</ref> and indicate that the present dataset is consistent with established findings on IC and fantasy play.

text.text: Building on this pattern, we propose an asymmetric organization: broader developmental and dispositional factors -school grade (lower grades), gender (girls), and fantasy orientation (higher scores) -are linked to the presence of IC, whereas NP shows at most a weak direct link with fantasy orientation and no link with school grade or gender, and is instead mainly contingent on the presence of IC.
In practical terms, NP was uncommon overall in our sample, yet the odds of NP were substantially higher when IC was present (OR ≈ 4.2; see Table 4).
text.formatted: In practical terms, NP was uncommon overall in our sample, yet the odds of NP were substantially higher when IC was present (OR ≈ 4.2; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Thus, NP is better viewed as a rare, idiosyncratic marker that co-occurs with IC, rather than as a direct expression of children's general fantasy play (quantified by the fantasy-orientation measure); the small effect of fantasy orientation on NP is consistent with NP sharing an imaginative basis with IC, but this effect was much smaller than that of IC itself.
We emphasize that this account is descriptive and does not imply causality.

The cross-sectional design and the low base rate of NP limit directional inferences; future longitudinal work and rare-event-appropriate analyses will be necessary to test whether NP merely co-occurs with IC or also contributes to the maintenance of IC in a subset of children.

We also note that the fantasy orientation score depends on coding decisions for frequent answers such as video games, which we treated as reality-oriented; when video games were instead treated as fantasy-oriented, the effect of fantasy orientation on NP was no longer significant, whereas the association between IC and NP was unchanged.

text.text: Furthermore, while the earlier research suggested that NP decreases as children grow older, we did not observe any significant age-related changes in our findings.
These discrepancies may be due to methodological differences.
Previous studies were based on children's own responses in a forced-choice consistency test (Matsuda et al., 2018), whereas the present study relied on parental reports.

text.text: Regarding IC, even if parents are not fully aware of the details, it is known that parental reports generally align with children's self-reports, making them a common approach in IC research (Taylor, 1999; Gleason, 2004; Bouldin and Pratt, 1999; Manosevitz et al., 1973; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: Since IC is correlated with fantasy orientation, it is considered to be closely related to children's daily play, making its manifestations in daily life easier to observe (Table 3; Moriguchi and Todo, 2017).

text.text: On the other hand, NP may be more introspective and less easily communicated to others.
To compute its prevalence more accurately, it is essential to rely on children's own responses, like the previous research, rather than solely relying on parental reports.
The second discrepancy, the absence of age-related change in NP, may partly reflect a lack of statistical power.
As illustrated in Figure 1c, the prevalence of NP appears to decrease consistently from 1st to 4th graders (ages 6-10), but a discontinuous change is noted among 5th and 6th graders.

text.text: Analyzing a larger sample might reveal an age-related decline in NP similar to the trend observed in grades 1-4.

Another possibility, which could account for both discrepancies, is that the two studies captured NP of different strength. Matsuda et al. (2018) found that the temporal consistency of NP was distributed continuously across children rather than dividing them into those with and without NP, and their forced-choice task could detect NP that a child would never mention spontaneously.

text.text: A parental report, by contrast, requires that the child's NP be expressed in everyday life clearly enough for the parent to notice it.
The 1.2% reported here may therefore correspond to the pronounced end of this spectrum, and NP that is pronounced enough to be visible to others may also be more stable across ages.
Although this interpretation is inferential, it is consistent with the fact that NP of this kind resembles a form of synesthesia, ordinal linguistic personification (OLP), as discussed below.

OLP is a form of synesthesia in which personality traits such as gender, age, or social roles are attributed to ordinal sequences such as letters, numbers, days, and months (Simner and Holenstein, 2007; Smilek et al., 2007).

text.text: Synesthetes with OLP give highly idiosyncratic but temporally consistent reports, e.g., "The number '3' is such a jerk!

He only thinks of himself" (Smilek et al., 2007), and OLP is found in around 1% of the adult population (Simner and Holenstein, 2007; Smilek et al., 2007; Amin et al., 2011; Sobczak-Edmans and Sagiv, 2013; Simner et al., 2016; Ward and Simner, 2022).

text.text: The NP reported by parents in this study resembles OLP in two further respects.
Its prevalence (1.2%) is close to that of OLP, and it did not change with school grade, whereas NP assessed with a forced-choice consistency test declines with age (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: Although age-related changes in OLP have not been studied directly, the prevalence of grapheme-color synesthesia is similar in 6-7-year-old children and adults (Simner et al., 2009), suggesting that the prevalence of OLP may also be stable across ages.

text.text: One reading of these observations is that NP in childhood is common but mostly weak, and that only in a small proportion of children it is pronounced enough to be noticed by parents and to persist; this pronounced NP may correspond to OLP in adults.
We stress that this is a hypothesis.

Whether parent-reported NP and adult OLP are the same phenomenon, and whether childhood NP is developmentally continuous with adult OLP, cannot be determined from the present data, and addressing these questions will require following the same children over time and combining parental reports with children's own accounts.
Moreover, although the previous study did obtain children's own responses, it focused on quantitative analyses (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: Given the high idiosyncrasy and complex variability of NP, qualitative analyses of children's own accounts will be essential, and future research should incorporate phenomenological methods designed for children (Philo, 2003).

text.text: In this study, we conducted a survey of parents to clarify the relationship between NP and children's fantasy play, using IC and fantasy orientation as indicators of everyday imaginative play.
Contrary to our hypothesis that NP is a developmental extension of IC, past IC did not predict current NP.
Instead, NP co-occurred with current IC: children with current ICs were about four times more likely to show NP.

Furthermore, IC was related to school grade, gender, and fantasy orientation, whereas NP showed no relation to school grade or gender and only a weak association with fantasy orientation, suggesting the asymmetric structure depicted in Figure 3.

text.text: The prevalence of parent-reported NP was lower than in previous research based on children's own responses, indicating that NP may vary in degree and that parental reports capture only its pronounced form (Matsuda et al., 2018).

text.text: Future research should combine parental reports with children's own accounts to gain a deeper understanding of this complex and idiosyncratic phenomenon.
